names.name: Azabache
names.th: อาซาบาเช (เครื่องรางหินเจ็ต)

etymology.root: Spanish azabache, from Arabic sabaj, the black stone — the amulet is named for its material, jet, and not for its shape
etymology.note: The fist form is also called a higa in Spanish, figa in Galician and Portuguese, and cigua in Asturleonese.

text.what: A piece of jet — fossil wood, black, warm to the touch, light in the hand — cut either as a small clenched fist with the thumb pushed between the first two fingers, or as a faceted black bead. Edward Tabor, writing in Hektoen International in 2023, measures the fist at about 8 mm long and the polyhedron at 3 to 4 mm across, each with a small red bead at the end of the chain. It is pinned to a baby's clothing or worn on a bracelet.
text.story:
Jet has been cut for amulets since the Neolithic, and in Spain the trade had a centre: the deposits are in Asturias, but by the end of the Middle Ages the working of jet religious objects and amulets was concentrated at Santiago de Compostela and sold to pilgrims on the Camino. The Asturian version handed to small children was, and is, a higa — the jet fist.

Tabor's account follows the object across the Atlantic. He traces the form to Muslim North Africa, citing Washington Irving's 1829 description of a comparable jet hand among "the Moors of Barbary", into Spain during the Moorish period of 711 to 1492, and then into the Spanish Caribbean colonies. Puerto Rican, Cuban and Dominican families put one on an infant within days of birth, and Tabor found that the practice continues into adulthood.

What parents told Tabor it is for is specific: the evil eye, and with it diarrhoea, respiratory infections, deformities, and above all sudden infant death. He reports that 29% of the wearers he surveyed had chosen the fist and 71% the polyhedron. He gives a price: US$3 to US$10 in a botánica, a folk-medicine shop, and US$9 to US$55 online at the time he wrote in 2023.

*Inference —* the red bead is worth noting. Red thread and red beads run with black stone across the whole Mediterranean, and the pairing here is the same pairing Naples makes with coral. This project files that as a family resemblance and not as a descent.
text.how: Cut and polished from jet, which is soft enough — Mohs 2.5 to 4 — to work with hand tools but chips if the carver pushes detail. Strung with a red bead, then pinned to the baby's shirt or fastened as a bracelet. It is given, usually by a grandmother or godparent, not bought by the wearer. Nothing in the sources read here describes a blessing; the giving is the act.
text.today: Sold in botánicas and online across the Spanish-speaking Caribbean, Spain and the United States. Tabor's 2023 figures — US$3 to US$10 in a shop, US$9 to US$55 online — are the last dated prices this project has read. Much of what is sold now is moulded black resin rather than cut jet; jet takes a brown streak on unglazed porcelain and burns like coal, which is how a buyer tells.

text_th.what: ชิ้นหินเจ็ต — ไม้ที่กลายเป็นฟอสซิล สีดำ จับแล้วรู้สึกอุ่น และเบามือ — เจียเป็นรูปกำปั้นเล็ก ๆ ที่สอดนิ้วโป้งไว้ระหว่างนิ้วชี้กับนิ้วกลาง หรือเจียเป็นลูกปัดสีดำหลายเหลี่ยม เอ็ดเวิร์ด เทเบอร์ (Edward Tabor) เขียนไว้ในวารสารเฮกโทเอนอินเตอร์เนชันแนล (Hektoen International) เมื่อ ค.ศ. 2023 ว่ากำปั้นยาวราว 8 mm และลูกปัดหลายเหลี่ยมกว้าง 3 ถึง 4 mm แต่ละชิ้นมีลูกปัดสีแดงเม็ดเล็กอยู่ที่ปลายสร้อย ใช้กลัดติดเสื้อผ้าของทารก หรือสวมกับสร้อยข้อมือ

dating.period: late medieval Iberia to the present
dating.label: c. 1400 to now
dating.note: 1400 is the 'end of the Middle Ages', when the cited source dates the great development of the Santiago de Compostela jet amulet trade. Jet amulets in Europe are far older — the earliest worked jet object is dated to 10,000 BCE — but the azabache as this record describes it is not.

object.made_by: jet cutters, historically the Santiago de Compostela workshops; the amulet is given by family, not bought by the wearer
object.note: 8 mm is Tabor's published figure for the fist form; he gives 3 to 4 mm for the polyhedron.

against.who: parents in Hispanic families, as surveyed by Edward Tabor
Tabor's respondents, who name sudden infant death first
against.note: also diarrhoea, respiratory infections and deformities

kin.as: the gesture this fist is a frozen copy of, and the reason it is also called a higa
the material the amulet is named after — azabache is simply the Spanish for it
the sign, filed in this atlas with the eye and the horn as things that catch a glance
the other charm put on a Latin American newborn against mal de ojo, in seed rather than stone
the Neapolitan answer: red coral instead of black jet, a horn instead of a fist
the red bead on the end of the chain, which runs with black stone right across the Mediterranean
the long read this belongs in — it goes on within days of birth
the tradition that carried it from Asturias to San Juan
the same harm answered with glass and an eye instead of jet and a hand

confusable_with.tell: figa names the gesture and any amulet of it, in any material; azabache names the jet the Spanish and Caribbean version is cut from, whatever shape it takes
